Threat_Name: Online brute-force password guessing
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service (reached via P1 Web Frontend)
Attack_Mechanism: Unbounded automated password guessing against the credential verification path: the attacker iterates candidate passwords for a known username until the verification result on DF4 indicates success; anti-automation is not specified by the architecture anywhere between the DF1 entry point and the DF3 verification cycle.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker obtains a valid username through enumeration (S1-RT-003), then scripts repeated login submissions on DF1, each carrying the same username with the next candidate password. P1 forwards every attempt on DF2, P2 executes a DF3 verification against DS1 for each, and no element in the drawn architecture limits attempt count or frequency. On the first successful verification the attacker receives a session token via DF6 and holds the account.
Security_Impact: Account takeover: one guessed password yields a valid session token on DF6, because the architecture specifies credential verification as the sole authentication factor and no second factor or step-up mechanism is drawn anywhere.
Architectural_Evidence: P2 is the sole authentication decision authority (stated assumption A1) and is anonymously reachable because DF1 crosses TB1 from the untrusted End User environment. The DF2 to DF3 verification cycle is unbounded in the drawn architecture: no anti-automation or attempt-limiting element is specified on any flow. OWASP A07 places anti-automation at exactly this point.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Architecture-grounded (DF1, DF2, DF3, TB1, A1); distinct from S1-RT-002, which is breadth-first replay of breached pairs rather than depth-first guessing; objectively matchable by attack pattern. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: the attacker presents a credential they do not own in order to be recognised as the account owner. Control-gap phrasing applied per rule 7: anti-automation is described as not specified, not as definitely absent. Evaluation note: if lockout-style anti-automation is implemented, it admits its own denial-of-access abuse vector, which is documented in the audit summary rather than retained as a separate architecture-level threat.

Threat_Name: Credential stuffing using breached credential corpora
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service
Attack_Mechanism: Distributed low-rate replay of externally breached username and password pairs across many accounts and sources, producing a per-account request pattern that per-account anti-automation, where implemented at all, does not detect.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker loads a corpus of breached credential pairs and submits each pair exactly once per account, distributed across many sources. Every account sees at most one failed DF3 verification, so any per-account attempt limit never trips; every password the victim reuses elsewhere yields a session token on DF6 for the attacker.
Security_Impact: Mass account takeover proportional to the password-reuse rate in the user population, with a session token issued on DF6 for every successful pair.
Architectural_Evidence: Like S1-RT-001 this exploits the anonymous reachability of DF1 across TB1 into P2, but the attack path is breadth-first across accounts rather than depth-first against one, producing a statistically different DF2 request pattern; OWASP treats stuffing and brute force as distinct techniques with distinct controls (breached-password screening versus attempt limiting).
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Distinct mechanism from S1-RT-001 (request pattern, detection signal and control all differ), so the pair is not merged. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: valid credentials of the real owner are used to impersonate them. Conditional phrasing applied: the presence of any attempt-limiting control is treated as unspecified, and the mechanism is stated as the pattern such controls fail to catch.

Threat_Name: Username and account enumeration
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; P1 Web Frontend
Attack_Mechanism: Differential response content, status or timing between existing and non-existing accounts turns the login and registration functions into an account-existence oracle whose signal crosses TB1 to the untrusted user environment.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker submits login attempts for candidate usernames with a fixed wrong password and compares the returned responses: an account-specific response for existing usernames versus a generic one for non-existing usernames, or a measurable timing difference carried by the DF4 result through P2 and P1, confirms which accounts exist before any guessing begins.
Security_Impact: Produces a validated target list that raises the yield of S1-RT-001 and S1-RT-002, and discloses membership information about identifiable persons.
Architectural_Evidence: The verification outcome produced on DF4 propagates back through P2 and P1 and crosses TB1 to the untrusted user environment; response uniformity is not specified by the architecture, so differentiating responses are an architecture-level exposure rather than an implementation accident. ASVS V2.2 requires uniform authentication responses at exactly this point.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. An enabler rather than a direct compromise (Severity Medium) but a distinct mechanism, a design-level response oracle, separable from S1-RT-019 (diagnostic-content disclosure) by inspection method and asset. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure: the leaked asset is account existence metadata. No implementation assumption is required: the oracle is defined by response differentiation across a drawn boundary.

Threat_Name: Authentication bypass through flawed authentication logic
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; P3 Session Management Module
Attack_Mechanism: Request manipulation reaches session creation on DF5 without a successful verification result: forged or mishandled verification state passed from P2 to P3, or direct invocation of the P3 session-creation function where it is independently reachable.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker submits crafted login content that causes P2 to pass an incomplete or mishandled verification result to the session-creation step, or invokes P3's session-creation function directly with a chosen identity; P3 issues a token on DF6 for an arbitrary account whose credentials were never verified against DS1.
Security_Impact: Complete authentication bypass: a valid session token is issued on DF6 for an arbitrary identity without any credential ever being verified, defeating the architecture's central property that P2 alone decides authentication.
Architectural_Evidence: Nothing in the drawn architecture forces DF5 to be preceded by a successful DF3/DF4 verification; the ordering constraint is an implementation convention rather than an enforced control, and the attacker input that drives the bypass enters across TB1 on DF1 and DF2. Stated assumption A1 makes P2 the sole authentication authority, so any path to DF5 around verification defeats a stated property with no drawn enforcement point. OWASP A04 (insecure design) applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: an unverified identity is accepted as an authenticated subject, which is the essence of spoofing; elevation of privilege is the downstream consequence when privileged accounts are targeted and is retained as a secondary note here only. Implementation-specific payload examples (type-confusion values) were removed; the mechanism is stated at the level of the unenforced DF3/DF4-before-DF5 ordering, which the drawn architecture fully supports. Severity Critical: the bypass mints sessions for arbitrary identities.

Threat_Name: Exposure of credentials in transit on the authentication paths
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend; P2 Authentication Service
Attack_Mechanism: Credentials in plaintext form traverse DF1 across TB1 and the internal DF2 leg, and confidentiality protection for these flows is not specified by the architecture; an actor positioned on either path reads submitted credentials.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An actor positioned on the communication path between the End User and P1, or between P1 and P2, reads the username and password of every login submission traversing DF1 and DF2. Any implementation-side persistence of flow content, which the architecture does not specify, would extend the same exposure to stored artefacts and is treated as conditional.
Security_Impact: Direct exposure of plaintext passwords, enabling immediate account takeover and cross-service reuse independent of any guessing.
Architectural_Evidence: DF1 and DF2 are the only flows in the model that carry plaintext credentials; DF1 crosses TB1 into the application; no confidentiality control for either flow is specified anywhere in the architecture, and under A6 that unspecified protection is itself the architecture-level finding. OWASP A02 applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite. The first-pass wording referenced transport-security mechanisms and logging artefacts that the architecture does not specify; the mechanism is now stated purely as unprotected credential-bearing flows across drawn boundaries, with persistence-based exposure phrased conditionally (rules 1 and 7). Distinct from S1-RT-001 and S1-RT-002: credentials are captured rather than guessed. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Injection into the credential verification exchange
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User credentials; password hashes; authentication decision
Attack_Mechanism: Untrusted input submitted on DF1 influences the verification request that P2 composes on DF3, altering what DS1 returns on DF4: the store result can be forced positive, or the exchange can be steered to return stored records beyond the intended lookup.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker submits a crafted username whose content changes the semantics of the DF3 verification request so that the DF4 response indicates success without the correct password; the same flaw is then steered to return stored credential records from DS1 instead of a single verification result.
Security_Impact: Simultaneous authentication bypass and mass disclosure of usernames and password hashes, the worst combined confidentiality and access-control outcome available in this architecture.
Architectural_Evidence: DF3, issued by P2 against DS1, is the only flow in the model where untrusted text that entered P1 across TB1 is transformed into a request interpreted by a higher-authority component across TB3; the taint path DF1 to DF2 to DF3 contains no validation or separation element, a confused-deputy condition at the TB3 crossing. OWASP A03 applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: implementation-specific injection constructs were removed, and the mechanism is stated as untrusted influence over the DF3/DF4 verification exchange, which the drawn architecture fully supports. Matching note: a candidate threat describing injection into the session-validation lookups on SF1/SF3 matches this entry, since the taint pattern and the mitigation class are identical. Primary STRIDE is Tampering: the integrity of the verification request is violated; bypass and extraction are consequences.

Threat_Name: Excessive database access scope across the application-to-database boundary
Affected_Components: Application services and store layer (P2, P3, P4 interacting with DS1, DS2, DS3)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User credentials; session tokens; LLM context repository
Attack_Mechanism: Access scoping at the TB3 crossing is not specified by the architecture: nothing requires that each service's store access be limited to the store it legitimately uses, so a compromised or defective service can read and write stores it never requires.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker who compromises P4 operates with its store access; because no per-service scoping is specified, the attacker reaches DS1 and DS2, password hashes and session tokens, although P4 legitimately requires only DS3.
Security_Impact: Compromise of any one application service yields read or write access to stores it does not need, so a defect in a lower-value service exposes authentication credentials in DS1 or session tokens in DS2.
Architectural_Evidence: TB3 exists to ensure that access to authentication and session data is subject to controlled authorisation. The model shows three distinct services crossing TB3 towards three distinct stores with disjoint legitimate needs: P2 to DS1 on DF3/DF4, P3 to DS2 on SF1, and P4 to DS3 on SF2; how access is scoped at that crossing is not specified, which is recorded as an architecture-level control gap.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with control-gap phrasing (rule 7): the entry states that scoping is not specified rather than claiming a specific misconfiguration. The entry makes no claim that the chatbot accesses the authentication databases: the architecture states the opposite, and access scoping is the control that keeps that stated property true under component compromise. Distinct from S1-RT-017, which addresses direct compromise of the session store itself. Primary STRIDE is Elevation of Privilege.

Threat_Name: Broken object-level authorisation on account data
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; P1 Web Frontend
Attack_Mechanism: An authenticated user substitutes another user's identifier in an account request, and P2 composes the DF3 request from the client-supplied identifier rather than from the identity bound to the authenticated session.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: After logging in normally, the attacker submits an account-information request naming a victim's identifier; P2 queries DS1 on DF3 using the supplied identifier and returns or modifies the victim's account record, because no element binds the DF3 access to the identity established at authentication.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised read or modification of other users' account information held in DS1.
Architectural_Evidence: Identity is established when DF4 returns a successful verification result, but the drawn architecture contains no enforcement element that binds subsequent DS1 access on DF3 to that established identity; authentication and authorisation are therefore separable in this design, and a request may cross TB1 with a valid session and still address another subject's data across TB3. OWASP A01 applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Elevation of Privilege: the attacker accesses an object belonging to another subject; information disclosure is the consequence and is noted as secondary here only. The grounding is absence-based (no authorisation-enforcement element is drawn), which is stated as a control gap rather than a definite flaw, hence Confidence Medium. Objectively matchable: any candidate threat describing unauthorised access to another user's account record through identifier substitution matches.

Threat_Name: Missing authorisation on the chatbot interface
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: LLM context; generated responses; provider quota
Attack_Mechanism: The chatbot interface is invoked directly rather than through the user interface, without presenting a valid session token, or the SF3 validation step is absent or advisory only, so the LLM pipeline is reachable without authentication.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An unauthenticated client calls the chatbot entry point directly, bypassing the web interface; P4 accepts the question on DF7, retrieves context on SF2, and P5 spends provider quota on DF9, all without a session token ever being presented or validated through SF3.
Security_Impact: Anonymous consumption of the downstream LLM pipeline, exposure of approved context and assistant behaviour to unauthenticated parties, and loss of per-user attribution for abuse.
Architectural_Evidence: DF7 runs from the untrusted End User directly to P4 and crosses TB1 independently of the DF1-to-DF6 authentication path, so P4 does not inherit any protection established at login; SF3, the session-token validation exchange between P3 and P4, is the only authorisation element on this path, and its enforcement strength is not specified. P4's stated responsibilities include no identity check of its own.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Elevation of Privilege: the attacker uses a protected application capability without any entitlement; no identity is forged, so Spoofing is not the primary violation. Classified as not LLM-specific: the defect is a missing access-control check on an application endpoint and would exist identically if P4 served static content. Conditional phrasing applied to the SF3 enforcement strength. Objectively matchable by the unauthenticated-reachability test.

Threat_Name: Cross-user context leakage between chatbot sessions
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User prompts; LLM context; generated responses
Attack_Mechanism: A shared or incorrectly keyed conversation-context buffer causes one user's prior questions or retrieved context to be incorporated into another user's prompt on DF8, or a concurrency defect causes a response on DF11 to be delivered to the wrong requester on DF12.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Two users question the chatbot concurrently; a context buffer keyed incorrectly under load causes user B's assembled prompt on DF8 to include user A's earlier authentication-related questions, and the generated answer is delivered to the wrong requester on DF12 with the application's authority.
Security_Impact: Disclosure of one user's authentication-related questions and identifiers to a different user, delivered with the application's authority.
Architectural_Evidence: P4 and P5 are single logical processes serving all users, and neither DF8 nor DF11 carries an explicit per-user key in the model; conversation context is required for coherent multi-turn answers yet is not represented as a data store in the architecture, so its isolation is not specified, and the leaked material crosses TB1 to the wrong subject on DF12.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. AI-specific because the leaked asset is accumulated AI context that exists only because prompts are assembled from conversational state. Distinct from S1-RT-026 (authorised aggregate interrogation, components behaving as designed) and from S1-RT-024 (egress to the provider): here the defect is internal keying or concurrency, and the isolation of the unrepresented context store is stated as an architecture-level gap. Confidence Medium for that reason.

Threat_Name: Session fixation on the authentication flow
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend Interface; P3 Session Management Module
Attack_Mechanism: Nothing in the architecture requires that the session identifier issued at the authentication transition be freshly derived: if an identifier the attacker already knows is accepted at DF5, P3 binds the victim's authenticated identity to that pre-existing value instead of generating a fresh one for DF6.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker supplies the victim with an authentication entry point that carries an attacker-chosen session identifier (the mechanism by which identifiers travel to the client is not specified by the architecture); the victim authenticates through it; P3 binds the authenticated identity to the known value, and from the moment login completes the attacker uses that identifier as the victim.
Security_Impact: The attacker holds a valid token for the victim's authenticated session from the moment login completes, without observing credentials, predicting a generated value, or intercepting any flow.
Architectural_Evidence: Token generation is an explicitly stated responsibility of P3, but the drawn flow set shows creation (DF5), issuance (DF6) and persistence (SF1) without any element requiring that the issued identifier be freshly derived at the authentication transition, so acceptance of a client-influenced identifier is an uncontrolled degree of freedom; ASVS V3.2 requires regeneration at every authentication transition.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: client-transport mechanisms for identifiers were removed, and the acceptance of a client-influenced identifier is phrased conditionally because identifier transport is not specified (rules 1 and 7). Retained separately from S1-RT-014, S1-RT-015 and S1-RT-016 because the attacker never acquires, computes or reuses a token: the victim authenticates onto an identifier the attacker already holds, a distinct control failure with a distinct mitigation. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing.

Threat_Name: Session token theft at the delivery and persistence crossings
Affected_Components: P3 Session Management Module; P1 Web Frontend; DS2 Session Storage
Attack_Mechanism: The bearer token is exposed at its two drawn crossings: at delivery to the client environment on DF6 across TB1, where protection of the token within the client context is not specified, and at persistence to DS2 on SF1 across TB3, where store-side protection is not specified; a captured token is presented as the victim.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Script executing in the victim's client environment, delivered for instance through S1-RT-033, reads the session token where it is exposed to client-side code and exfiltrates it; the attacker presents the token from their own client and operates as the victim for the remaining token lifetime.
Security_Impact: Full session hijack: the attacker acts as the victim without possessing credentials, defeating password strength and every login-time control.
Architectural_Evidence: The session token is a bearer secret exposed at two distinct boundaries with two distinct control sets: it crosses TB1 on DF6 when delivered to the client, and TB3 on SF1 when persisted to DS2; neither crossing has a specified protection, and no element in the model protects either leg specifically.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: implementation-specific client-side protections were removed and replaced with the unspecified-protection phrasing for both drawn crossings (rules 1 and 7). Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: the primary violation is unauthorised use of the victim's authenticated session; the capture enabling it is information disclosure, noted as secondary. Both crossings are kept so that a partial mitigation at one boundary is not mistaken for coverage. Severity Critical: terminal node of the injection-to-takeover chain anchored by S1-RT-033.

Threat_Name: Predictable or weakly generated session tokens
Affected_Components: P3 Session Management Module
Attack_Mechanism: Unpredictability of the tokens that P3 generates is not a property specified by the architecture; if issued identifiers are derivable from observable values, an attacker can compute valid tokens belonging to other users from samples exposed on DF6.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The attacker creates several accounts and logs into each, collecting the tokens issued on DF6; the values reveal a derivable pattern, from which the attacker computes a currently valid token for a victim and presents it directly, without any victim interaction or activity on the login path.
Security_Impact: Session hijack at scale with no victim interaction and no activity on the login path, therefore invisible to authentication monitoring.
Architectural_Evidence: Generating session tokens is an explicitly stated responsibility of P3, so token unpredictability is a property of a named process in this architecture; the generated value is exposed on DF6 across TB1, which is what gives an attacker the samples needed to infer the generator, and the unpredictability requirement is not specified anywhere. ASVS V3.2 applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with conditional phrasing (rule 7): the entry states that unpredictability is not specified and conditions the attack on derivable identifiers, rather than asserting a weak generator. The failure is generation-side and therefore distinct from the delivery-side and storage-side exposure of S1-RT-014, with which it is not merged. Likelihood Low: strong generation is the implementation norm, but the impact scale keeps severity High and the entry evaluable.

Threat_Name: Token replay and absent session invalidation
Affected_Components: P3 Session Management Module; DS2 Session Storage
Attack_Mechanism: The model contains session creation (DF5, DF6), persistence (SF1) and validation (SF3) but no flow by which a session is terminated or a DS2 record removed; token lifetime is therefore unbounded in the drawn architecture, and a token that leaves the victim's control remains usable.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A token stolen through S1-RT-014 continues to work after the victim logs out (no logout or revocation flow exists in the model), after a password change, and after the attacker's presence is suspected; the DS2 record is never removed, so the hijacked session persists indefinitely.
Security_Impact: Indefinite persistence of a compromised session: logout and password change fail to evict an attacker who already holds a token.
Architectural_Evidence: This threat is justified by an absence in the drawn architecture rather than by any element: no termination or revocation flow exists, so no element is responsible for invalidation and token lifetime is unbounded by construction; this is stated as an architecture-level gap, not as a claim about implementation behaviour.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: the mechanism is replay of a captured authenticator, which is spoofing of the session owner; elevation of privilege is secondary. Implementation-specific token-design clauses were removed; the absence-based grounding needs no assumption beyond the drawn flow set. The fixation overlap remains correctly separated: S1-RT-013 handles pre-authentication binding, this entry handles post-issuance lifecycle. Confidence Medium: absence-based grounding.

Threat_Name: Session storage compromise and record tampering
Affected_Components: DS2 Session Storage; P3 Session Management Module
Attack_Mechanism: Protection of DS2 itself is not specified beyond the TB3 boundary; an attacker reaching the store directly can insert session records that map an attacker-held token to a victim identity, or read stored tokens in bulk.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker reaches DS2 directly behind TB3 and inserts a record binding a token value they control to a victim's identity; subsequent SF3 validation of that token succeeds, and the attacker operates as the victim without ever interacting with P2.
Security_Impact: Mass session hijack across the user population and forgery of authenticated sessions without any interaction with the authentication service.
Architectural_Evidence: Applying STRIDE-per-element to DS2 yields tampering and information-disclosure cases not covered by the delivery-oriented S1-RT-014, because the attack occurs entirely behind TB3 on the SF1 path; TB3 is drawn precisely to mark the store boundary, and the store's own protection is not specified by the architecture.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with control-gap phrasing: the store's protection is described as unspecified rather than weak. Primary STRIDE is Tampering: the distinctive capability is forgery of stored session state. To prevent double-crediting, the bulk token-extraction leg is cross-referenced to the storage side of S1-RT-014 rather than restated, and the over-privileged-access vector is carried by S1-RT-009. Likelihood Low: requires direct store-level compromise behind TB3.

Threat_Name: Mass disclosure of the user database
Affected_Components: DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User credentials; password hashes; account information (PII)
Attack_Mechanism: Unauthorised bulk read of DS1's contents through any available path: influence over the verification exchange through S1-RT-008, cross-store access through S1-RT-009, or direct compromise of the store, whose own protection is not specified by the architecture.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Through the injection flaw of S1-RT-008 the verification exchange is steered to return stored account records; the attacker obtains usernames, salted password hashes and account information for the entire population. Password policy and hash-function configuration beyond salting are not specified; if either is weak, the disclosed records are additionally recoverable offline, which is recorded as a conditional amplifier and a control gap.
Security_Impact: Catastrophic and irreversible disclosure of the entire credential population, with statutory breach-notification obligations and cross-service reuse harm to users.
Architectural_Evidence: DS1 is the highest-value asset in the model and sits entirely behind TB3, reachable through the DF3 and DF4 pair; STRIDE-per-element mandates an information-disclosure entry for every data store, and the store-direct compromise path of this entry is not carried by any other entry.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained as the store-level disclosure entry. Challenged under rule 3 as potentially a mere consequence of S1-RT-008 and S1-RT-009, and retained deliberately: the asset-level consequence, the detection strategy and the regulatory obligations are properties of the store, and the store-direct path is unique to this entry. Modification: implementation-specific exposure vectors for stored copies of the database were removed as unspecified technologies, and the weak-policy/hash amplification previously carried by a separate entry is absorbed here as a conditional note and cross-listed as a control gap. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Verbose error and diagnostic disclosure
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend; P2 Authentication Service; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Data_Flows: DF6 and DF1 response paths; DF10 and DF12 error paths
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: System configuration metadata; prompt content; internal identifiers
Attack_Mechanism: Internal implementation detail is propagated to responses returned across TB1: diagnostic or configuration content generated in P1 or P2, and provider-side error content received by P5 on DF10, reaches the untrusted user environment, and response-content discipline is not specified by the architecture.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An unhandled failure at P2 causes internal diagnostic content, including a fragment of the verification request, to be returned through P1 to the attacker; separately, a provider error body received on DF10 that embeds the submitted prompt is relayed verbatim on DF12, carrying prompt content back across TB1.
Security_Impact: Reconnaissance that materially accelerates S1-RT-004 and S1-RT-008 crafting, with occasional direct exposure of sensitive detail embedded in error content.
Architectural_Evidence: The threat is anchored to two boundary crossings: on TB1, content generated by P1 and P2 returns to the untrusted user environment on the DF1 and DF6 response paths; on TB2, P5 receives provider error bodies on DF10, and relaying them on DF12 would carry prompt content back across TB1; no response-normalisation element is specified.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: implementation-specific diagnostic artefacts were generalised to internal diagnostic or configuration content. Distinct from S1-RT-003: that entry is a design-level response oracle (differential existence signalling), this one is diagnostic-content disclosure; different assets, different inspection method, different mitigation. Classified not LLM-specific: the defect is classical response discipline regardless of whether the upstream service is a language model. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Exposure of the external service API credential
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service
Attack_Mechanism: The provider authentication material that P5 must hold to perform the DF9 crossing is exposed: its storage and handling are not specified by the architecture, and any exposure yields a secret that authenticates the application to EE2.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The credential material held at P5 is exposed through an implementation artefact, whose nature the architecture does not specify; the attacker recovers it and submits prompts under the application's provider identity, consuming quota and impersonating the application toward EE2.
Security_Impact: Unbounded chargeable use of the organisation's provider account, attacker access to any provider-side data associated with the credential, and complete loss of attribution for prompts submitted under it.
Architectural_Evidence: P5 is the single process performing the TB2 crossing on DF9, so the credential it must hold is a boundary-attached secret; the DS3 specification explicitly lists API keys among the secrets that must not reside in the context repository, establishing that an API credential exists as a system asset. OWASP A02 applies to secrets of this kind.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: implementation-specific exposure channels were replaced by the unspecified-storage phrasing (rules 1 and 7). The credential's existence is grounded in the DS3 exclusion note together with DF9's stated purpose of sending prompts to the external provider on the application's behalf. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure: the credential is the disclosed asset, and its abuse is the impact. Not LLM-specific: classical secret exposure.

Threat_Name: Unspecified attribution of security-relevant actions
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; P3 Session Management Module; P4 AI Chatbot Component; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Attribution and accountability of security-relevant actions
Attack_Mechanism: No audit or attribution mechanism is specified for the security-relevant actions of P2, P3, P4 and P5, so performed actions cannot be attributed to a subject and cannot be contradicted after the fact.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker completes an account takeover; when the action is later disputed, no specified mechanism can show which subject performed the involved authentication attempts, session issuances or chatbot requests, and the attacker can credibly deny having performed them.
Security_Impact: Attack campaigns proceed without attribution, incident scope cannot be reconstructed, actions cannot be bound to a subject, and disputes cannot be resolved.
Architectural_Evidence: STRIDE assigns repudiation to every process, and the events requiring attribution are generated by P2, P3, P4 and P5 at all three boundaries: authentication attempts reaching P2 across TB1 on DF1 and DF2, data egress from P5 across TB2 on DF9, and privileged access by P2 and P3 across TB3 on DF3 and SF1; the drawn architecture contains no audit element, so attribution is not specified.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with strict control-gap phrasing: the entry states that attribution is not specified (rule 7) and assumes no particular logging infrastructure (rule 1); the threat is the repudiation exposure that follows from the drawn architecture itself. Primary STRIDE is Repudiation, a native single-category fit and the sole repudiation entry in the baseline. Severity Medium as an enabler whose harm materialises through the entries it shields.

Threat_Name: Direct prompt injection
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component (prompt assembly); P5 LLM Integration Service; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: LLM context; system instructions; generated responses
Attack_Mechanism: User input submitted on DF7 is interpreted by the model as instruction rather than data: P4 assembles the untrusted text together with trusted system instructions and approved context into a single prompt that crosses TB2 on DF9, with no instruction-data separation anywhere in the pipeline.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The user submits an instruction to disregard prior instructions and reveal the configuration; P4 concatenates it into the prompt on DF8, P5 sends it on DF9, and the model complies within its DF10 response, which P1 displays to the user on DF12 as an assistant answer.
Security_Impact: Disclosure of instructions and approved context present in the prompt window, generation of content that violates intended topic restrictions, and production of attacker-chosen text that the application presents as authoritative guidance.
Architectural_Evidence: DF7 carries arbitrary untrusted text across TB1 into P4 (stated assumption A5: user inputs may be malicious), and the assembled prompt crosses TB2 on DF9 as one undifferentiated sequence, a confused-deputy condition at the prompt-assembly step; MITRE ATLAS records this vector as AML.T0051.000 (Direct Prompt Injection).
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained unchanged in substance. Architecture-grounded entirely in drawn flows and stated assumptions; the highest-likelihood AI-specific entry. Severity High rather than Critical because the architecture grants the model no authority: it cannot authenticate users, modify accounts or reach DS1 and DS2, so direct impact is bounded by disclosure of prompt content and manipulation of returned text; its role as the entry point for the chains through S1-RT-033 and S1-RT-034 is where the greater risk lies. Primary STRIDE is Tampering.

Threat_Name: Indirect prompt injection through the context repository
Affected_Components: DS3 Knowledge Base and Context Repository; P4 AI Chatbot Component
Affected_Data_Flows: SF2, DF8, DF9, DF10, DF11, DF12
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: LLM context; generated responses; integrity of published guidance
Attack_Mechanism: An actor able to influence the content of DS3 embeds instructions inside otherwise legitimate documentation; every subsequent user whose query retrieves that document on SF2 has the embedded instruction acted upon on their behalf inside the prompt.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An actor with influence over DS3 content, whether through a compromised content-author account or an unreviewed automated import, adds an instruction to a widely retrieved article directing users to verify their identity at an attacker-controlled destination; every user whose question retrieves that article receives the manipulated guidance with the application's authority.
Security_Impact: Persistent and victim-agnostic manipulation of assistant behaviour: users can be directed towards attacker-controlled destinations, prompted to disclose authentication information, or given deliberately weakened guidance.
Architectural_Evidence: The injection point is a data store located inside TB3 rather than the user input field, so input-validation controls on DF7 do not detect it; DS3 is the only store in the model whose integrity requirement exceeds its confidentiality requirement, because its contents are retrieved on SF2 and interpreted as part of the instruction stream; the DS3 write path is not a numbered flow in the architecture, which is recorded as a precondition and control gap. MITRE ATLAS records this vector as AML.T0051.001 (Indirect Prompt Injection).
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Blast radius is all users, persistently, which makes this the highest-leverage AI-specific threat in the model. The write-path authorisation weakness is deliberately folded in as a precondition rather than kept separate, because it has no security consequence in this architecture except through prompt assembly. Confidence Medium because the precondition concerns an unmodelled write path, which is stated as a gap. Primary STRIDE is Tampering.

Threat_Name: Sensitive information disclosure to the external LLM provider
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component (prompt assembly); P5 LLM Integration Service (egress); EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User prompts; LLM context; account identifiers; prohibited material (passwords, password hashes, session tokens, secrets)
Attack_Mechanism: Prompt assembly at P4 sends more than the sanitised prompt the specification permits: design-time over-inclusion of identifiers or account state, unscoped retrieval on SF2 pulling internal material from DS3, user-pasted credentials on DF7 forwarded verbatim, and prohibited material such as session tokens carried into the prompt through the validation and context paths.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A user pastes their password into the chat while asking for help, or a session token presented towards validation is captured into context at P4 and attached to the next prompt; the material crosses TB2 on DF9 to EE2, leaves the application's security control, and cannot be retracted.
Security_Impact: Irreversible disclosure of context, personal data and prohibited material to a third party whose handling practices are outside the organisation's audit scope, directly violating the specification's egress prohibition.
Architectural_Evidence: TB2 exists precisely because prompts and contextual information leave the application's security control, and the specification states that only sanitised prompts and authorisation-approved context may be sent to EE2, explicitly prohibiting passwords, password hashes, session tokens and secrets; this entry tests exactly that stated property, and no minimisation or allow-listing element is drawn between context assembly and DF9.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained, including the first-pass extension: the egress of explicitly prohibited material, in particular session tokens and password hashes carried through the validation and context paths, is an explicit part of the mechanism because the specification names these prohibitions and no other entry tests them. The SF2 scope-control failure remains folded here (same asset, same boundary, same mitigation). Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure. It is the only confidentiality loss in the model with no application-side remedy after the fact.

Threat_Name: System prompt and instruction extraction
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; EE2 External LLM Provider
Attack_Mechanism: Iterative elicitation causes the instruction preamble that travels with every prompt to be reproduced in responses: verbatim repetition requests, configuration summaries, and translation or rephrasing variants.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Over several turns the attacker requests verbatim repetition of preceding text and rephrasing variants until the guardrail preamble appears in a DF10 response and reaches the user on DF12, revealing the assistant's instructions and any configuration embedded in them.
Security_Impact: Reveals the guardrail logic and therefore the means to bypass it, enabling more reliable exploitation of S1-RT-022, and may expose internal procedures, model details or business rules embedded in the preamble.
Architectural_Evidence: The extraction request enters P4 on DF7 across TB1, is incorporated into the prompt that crosses TB2 on DF9, and the disclosed instruction text returns on DF10 and DF12; extraction requires conversation only, no component compromise. MITRE ATLAS catalogues this technique as AML.T0056 (LLM Meta Prompt Extraction).
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Retained separately from S1-RT-022 because the asset and the mitigation differ: the countermeasure is to treat the prompt as public, remove sensitive material from it and enforce controls outside the model, rather than to filter input; retaining it separately also prevents a candidate model that states only prompt injection from being credited with this distinct outcome. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure. Severity Medium: informational loss that primarily enables other entries. No implementation assumption is involved.

Threat_Name: Disclosure of knowledge-base and context content through the assistant
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; DS3 Knowledge Base and Context Repository; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Approved documentation corpus; chatbot context information; generated responses
Attack_Mechanism: Incremental targeted interrogation causes the model to reproduce and aggregate retrieved context in its answers; no element compares the retrieved context against the entitlement of the requesting identity, since SF2 is modelled as retrieval for relevance, not as an authorisation decision.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker asks many narrow questions about internal procedure names, policy details, naming conventions, support contacts and administrative workflows; the assistant retrieves approved documentation on SF2 for each and assembles, over many turns, a curated internal reconnaissance dossier delivered on DF12.
Security_Impact: A curated internal reconnaissance dossier obtained through the trusted interface, materially raising the yield of S1-RT-003 and targeted attacks, and disclosure of context material beyond the entitlement of the asking user.
Architectural_Evidence: Content crosses TB3 outbound on SF2 into the prompt and returns to the user across TB1 on DF12, and between those crossings no element performs an entitlement check; every component behaves as designed, and the disclosure arises because unbounded interrogation of the assistant is itself an authorised action whose aggregate exceeds any single intended disclosure.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. The distinctness analysis is confirmed: S1-RT-024 concerns egress towards EE2, S1-RT-025 concerns the model's hidden instructions, S1-RT-012 concerns a concurrency defect, and this entry concerns authorised aggregate disclosure, so no merge is warranted. Severity Medium stands: DS3 is defined as approved documentation, which bounds corpus sensitivity. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Conditional provider-side exposure of submitted prompts
Affected_Components: EE2 External LLM Provider
Attack_Mechanism: Conditional provider-side risk: if the external provider retains, logs or reuses the content submitted on DF9, retention practices being outside the application's control and not specified by the architecture, then a later provider-side exposure event affects the entire history of submitted prompts and context.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: If DF9 content is retained provider-side and is later exposed through a provider-side event, the authentication-related questions of the user population, together with any over-included context from S1-RT-024, become known to the attacker; no application-side action can retract or bound the exposure.
Security_Impact: Long-tail confidentiality loss across the history of DF9 traffic, loss of control over deletion, and the possibility that content submitted by one user surfaces in a response returned to another user.
Architectural_Evidence: EE2 is drawn as an entity beyond TB2, outside the application's security control, specifically to force reasoning about what happens after successful delivery; the architecture specifies no retention practices, so the provider-side behaviour is stated conditionally and the entry records the consequence if that condition holds.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with conditional phrasing throughout, exactly as rule 7 requires for provider-side behaviour: the entry states the conditional exposure rather than asserting that the provider retains prompts. The cross-user surfacing case stays folded as a realisation of the same conditional exposure. Severity remains High because the triggering egress on DF9 is structural and the consequence is irreversible, while Likelihood is Medium because realisation requires both the unspecified retention behaviour and a secondary provider-side event. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Denial of service against the authentication service
Affected_Components: P2 Authentication Service; DS1 User Database
Attack_Mechanism: Volumetric flooding of the login and registration functions on DF1 and DF2 saturates P2's processing and its access to DS1; verification against salted password hashes is a deliberate computation, so each flooded request imposes asymmetric work on the service.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker floods DF1 with login attempts from distributed sources; every attempt triggers a DF3 verification computation and store access at P2; capacity saturates and legitimate users cannot authenticate, which is a full-system outage because every other capability depends on holding a session.
Security_Impact: Legitimate users cannot authenticate; because every other capability depends on holding a session, an authentication outage is effectively a full-system outage.
Architectural_Evidence: The threat is located on the DF1 to DF2 to DF3 request path read as a resource path across TB1 and TB3; no rate-limiting, queueing or load-isolation element is specified on any of these flows, and salted hash verification is by construction a deliberate computation at P2, which the architecture itself specifies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a technology-neutral rewrite: capacity terminology was generalised and the cost-asymmetry argument now rests only on the specified salted-hash verification rather than on any assumed hashing technology. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service. Severity Medium, Likelihood Medium: launching the attempt is trivial, sustained impact depends on capacity handling that the architecture does not specify.

Threat_Name: External LLM provider unavailability or degradation
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service; P4 AI Chatbot Component; EE2 External LLM Provider
Attack_Mechanism: Provider outage, rate-limit rejection or degraded latency on the synchronous DF9/DF10 pair leaves the chatbot unable to answer; how P5 handles provider non-response is not specified by the architecture, so waiting behaviour and its capacity consequences are implementation-dependent.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The external provider suffers an extended outage; the DF10 responses never arrive, and the chatbot returns errors or nothing to every user. Whether the failure propagates further depends on runtime topology, which the drawn architecture does not establish.
Security_Impact: Loss of the chatbot capability. Propagation of the outage into the authentication path through shared request-handling capacity is possible in some deployments but is not established by the drawn architecture and is therefore recorded as conditional.
Architectural_Evidence: TB2 marks a dependency that the organisation can neither control nor repair, and DF9 and DF10 form a synchronous request-response pair across it; the drawn architecture establishes the direct consequence, chatbot loss, but contains no evidence about shared runtime capacity between the chatbot pipeline and the authentication path.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with conditional scoping. The first-pass claim that the outage propagates into authentication rested on a runtime assumption the architecture does not make; under rule 1 it is removed from the impact and recorded as a conditional clarification. The baseline keeps the direct, drawn consequence. AI-specific because the dependency exists solely to obtain generated responses from an external model. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service.

Threat_Name: Unbounded consumption of the LLM processing pipeline
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; P5 LLM Integration Service; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Chatbot availability; provider quota; operating budget
Attack_Mechanism: High-frequency questions, inputs sized to fill the model context window, or prompts constructed to maximise generated output length drive the variable per-token cost of DF9; no metering, quota or cost control is specified on the DF7 to DF9 chain, and the path may be driven anonymously where S1-RT-011 applies.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A script submits maximum-length questions crafted to elicit maximum-length answers at line rate on DF7; the cost of each DF9 crossing scales with input and output tokens; the provider quota and budget exhaust, denying the chatbot to legitimate users through billing rather than through capacity.
Security_Impact: Degraded or unavailable chatbot, processing backlog in P4 and P5, direct chargeable cost, and exhaustion of the provider quota, which then denies service through billing rather than through capacity.
Architectural_Evidence: DF7 crosses TB1 into P4 with no stated size or rate constraint, and the DF9 crossing of TB2 has a cost that is variable and attacker-influenced because it scales with token counts; request-count limiting alone is structurally insufficient and token-budget limiting is required, which no element provides.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Capacity exhaustion and chargeable-cost exhaustion remain combined in one entry because they share the DF7-to-DF9 attack path and the same control class, and the distinction is one of impact type rather than of mechanism, so splitting them would violate rule 4. AI-specific because the cost driver is per-token model inference, with no analogue in the classical flows. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service. Likelihood High: no metering is drawn and the entry point is trivially reachable.

Threat_Name: Hallucinated authentication guidance
Affected_Components: EE2 External LLM Provider; P4 AI Chatbot Component
Attack_Mechanism: Without any adversary, the model produces confident but incorrect content; the response crosses TB2 on DF10, passes through P5 and P4 with no element responsible for verifying factual accuracy, and is displayed on DF12 inside the trusted application interface.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A user asks how to regain access after a lockout; the model confidently describes a non-existent procedure or fabricated contact destination; the user, unable to verify the guidance elsewhere, follows it and discloses authentication information through the incorrect channel or to a destination an attacker may subsequently register.
Security_Impact: Users are guided towards insecure behaviour, including disclosing authentication information through an incorrect channel or acting on a fabricated destination.
Architectural_Evidence: No adversary or boundary violation is required: every component behaves as engineered, yet the security outcome is negative; the content originates at EE2, crosses TB2 inbound on DF10, and crosses TB1 to the user on DF12 without any accuracy-control element, which the architecture does not specify.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. This is the one threat class in the model with no classical STRIDE analogue, and the primary STRIDE field carries the single label Tampering under an explicitly extended interpretation, loss of integrity of generated information, with that rationale stated here as the single-category rule requires. The user-trust amplification folded into this entry in the first pass remains: users cannot easily verify guidance they depend on. Severity Medium: unintentional, not reliably targetable, correctable through verification against authoritative documentation. Likelihood High: intrinsic model behaviour.

Threat_Name: Insecure handling of generated output
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; P1 Web Frontend
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated responses; session tokens; user browser context
Attack_Mechanism: Content that crossed TB2 inbound on DF10 is displayed by P1 on DF12; output encoding or content separation at the rendering step is not specified by the architecture, so attacker-influenced active content executes in the victim's authenticated client context.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Through S1-RT-022 or S1-RT-023 the attacker induces the model to emit active content in its answer; P1 displays the response without separation; the content executes in the victim's authenticated session, reads the session token as described in S1-RT-014, and completes a full account takeover.
Security_Impact: Execution of attacker-influenced content in the victim's authenticated client context, leading to theft of the session token, actions performed on the victim's behalf, or presentation of a fabricated credential-harvesting form inside the legitimate interface.
Architectural_Evidence: Stated assumption A4 declares external LLM output untrusted, yet no encoding or content-separation element is specified between DF10 and the DF12 rendering; the architecture's containment rests on the model reaching no database, but its output is displayed to the user, so an advisory-only component still provides a path to session compromise. OWASP LLM05 applies.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Tampering: attacker-influenced content enters the display path unmodified; the elevation of privilege and session compromise are consequences and are noted as secondary. Severity Critical stands because the chain terminates in full account takeover. This entry is the practical realisation of unintended authority for a guidance-only assistant: generated content becomes executable authority in the authenticated client context, which is how the excessive-authority concern manifests in this architecture.

Threat_Name: Delivery of attacker-authored instructions through the assistant
Affected_Components: P4 AI Chatbot Component; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated responses; user credentials; user security behaviour
Attack_Mechanism: Through poisoned context as described in S1-RT-023, direct injection as in S1-RT-022, or provider substitution as in S1-RT-036, the returned answer instructs the user to act against their own interest, and the trusted DF12 delivery channel converts the text into an effective attack.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A poisoned knowledge-base article causes the assistant to tell users to confirm their identity at an attacker-controlled destination; users comply at a rate substantially higher than external phishing, because the instruction arrives inside the trusted application interface in direct response to their own question.
Security_Impact: Disclosure of credentials or authentication information to the attacker, delivered through the application's own trusted channel.
Architectural_Evidence: The harmful content enters across TB2 on DF10 and reaches the user across TB1 on DF12; the delivery channel's organisational authority is what converts generated text into an effective attack, and no output-side content policy or destination allow-listing element is specified at P4.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained. Primary STRIDE is Tampering: attacker-chosen content is substituted for legitimate guidance in the delivery path; the authority-lending property of the DF12 channel, a spoofing-like characteristic, is noted as secondary. Retained separately from S1-RT-032 because the content is intentional and attacker-chosen rather than accidental, which changes the required control from model accuracy to output-side policy enforcement; the two are independently identifiable and matchable, so rule 3 does not merge them. The user-trust amplification folded into this entry in the first pass remains.

Threat_Name: Compromise or substitution of the external model service
Affected_Components: EE2 External LLM Provider; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User prompts; LLM context; generated responses
Attack_Mechanism: The DF9/DF10 exchange depends on the identity and integrity of the responder beyond TB2, and no mechanism verifying that the responder is the intended external service is specified by the architecture; if EE2 is substituted or compromised, prompts are harvested and responses are attacker-controlled.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The communication that P5 sends on DF9 is answered by an attacker-controlled replacement of the intended external service, the substitution path lying outside the drawn architecture; every prompt is harvested, realising the S1-RT-024 exposure actively, and every DF10 response is attacker-authored, weaponising S1-RT-033 and S1-RT-034 for all users. An unannounced provider-side model or behaviour change has the same effect without any application modification.
Security_Impact: Interception of every prompt crossing TB2 together with control of every response returned on DF10, converting the assistant into an attacker-controlled channel for all users.
Architectural_Evidence: P5 is the only element that performs the TB2 crossing, so any verification of the external service's identity and integrity must concentrate at that single process, and no such verification is specified; EE2 is not merely a service the application calls but the source of content the application redistributes to users across TB1 on DF12. MITRE ATLAS frames the substitution angle as ML supply chain compromise.
Expert_Justification: Final audit: retained with a trust-boundary-level rewrite: infrastructure-specific substitution mechanisms were removed (rules 1), and the mechanism is now stated as the unspecified verification of the responder's identity beyond TB2, with the substitution path declared to lie outside the drawn architecture. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: the trusted external entity is impersonated or substituted; control of the responses is the consequence and is noted as secondary. Likelihood Low: requires a substantial external compromise, but the impact spans the whole user base, keeping severity High.
